questiontext.text:
River pollution: does land use matter?

An environmental scientist collected samples at 24 river sites, classified as forest, agricultural or industrial. All pollutant concentrations are measured in mg/L.

Download the CSV. Its columns are Site, Distance_km, Land_use and Concentration_mg_L.

Download the data

A. Recognising factors

Which variable identifies the type of surrounding land use?

[[input:ans_factor]] [[validation:ans_factor]]

How many levels does this factor have?

[[input:ans_levels]] [[validation:ans_levels]]

B. Comparing groups

Calculate the mean concentration for each land-use category. Give each answer to two decimal places.

Forest: [[input:ans_forest]] [[validation:ans_forest]] mg/L

Agricultural: [[input:ans_agricultural]] [[validation:ans_agricultural]] mg/L

Industrial: [[input:ans_industrial]] [[validation:ans_industrial]] mg/L

C. Choosing a graph

You want to compare the distribution of pollutant concentrations across the three land-use categories (Forest, Agricultural and Industrial). Which graph is most appropriate for this purpose?

Select an option to preview that graph immediately. You can change your selection before submitting your answer.

[[input:ans_graph]] [[validation:ans_graph]]

generalfeedback.text:
Worked solution

Land_use is a factor with three levels: Forest, Agricultural and Industrial. Concentration and distance are numerical variables.

All concentrations are already in mg/L. Calculate the mean within each land-use category.

Land useMean (mg/L)
Forest{@ta_mean_forest@}
Agricultural{@ta_mean_agricultural@}
Industrial{@ta_mean_industrial@}

Comparing the three factor levels: side-by-side boxplots

Each boxplot summarises the distribution of pollutant concentrations within one land-use category. The coloured box extends from the lower to the upper quartile; the line inside it marks the median. Whiskers here extend to the minimum and maximum. The black diamond marks the mean calculated above.

[[jsxgraph width="650px" height="410px"]] var groups=[{#forest_clean#},{#agricultural_clean#},{#industrial_clean#}]; var labels=['Forest','Agricultural','Industrial']; var colours=['#2563eb','#16a34a','#dc2626']; var all=groups[0].concat(groups[1],groups[2]); var lo=Math.min.apply(null,all),hi=Math.max.apply(null,all); var pad=Math.max(1,(hi-lo)*0.18); var board=JXG.JSXGraph.initBoard(divid,{ boundingbox:[0.35,hi+pad,3.65,lo-pad], axis:false,showCopyright:false,showNavigation:false, keepaspectratio:false }); function quantile(a,p){ var v=a.slice().sort(function(x,y){return x-y;}); var h=(v.length-1)*p,j=Math.floor(h); return v[j]+(v[Math.min(j+1,v.length-1)]-v[j])*(h-j); } for(var g=0;g<3;g++){ var a=groups[g],x=g+1; var q1=quantile(a,0.25),med=quantile(a,0.5),q3=quantile(a,0.75); var mn=Math.min.apply(null,a),mx=Math.max.apply(null,a); var total=0; for(var i=0;iWhy boxplots? Land use is a factor: its three levels define separate groups. Side-by-side boxplots allow us to compare their medians, spreads and ranges. The black diamonds connect this graph to the three group means calculated earlier. A scatterplot of distance against concentration addresses a different question; a histogram combines the groups; connecting categorical groups with a line suggests an artificial continuity.

6. Observations, variables and factor levels

The CSV contains 24 observations (one per sampling site), four variables (Site, Distance_km, Land_use and Concentration_mg_L), and three levels of Land_use (Forest, Agricultural and Industrial).
